statement: Every separable real [normed space](c:normed-space) $X$ has a linear map $T\colon X \to C[0,1]$ with $\|Tx\|_\infty = \|x\|$, where $C[0,1]$ is the space of [continuous functions](c:c-0-1) on $[0,1]$. When $X$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space), the image of $T$ is closed.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a real [normed space](c:normed-space).
The space $X$ has a countable dense subset.

conclusion: There is a linear isometry $T\colon X \to C[0,1]$, and its image is a closed subspace when $X$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space).

proofs.name: Dual ball and Cantor set
proofs.slogan: Embed $X$ in the continuous functions on its dual ball, pull back along a Cantor set, then extend linearly across the gaps.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for real scalars. A closed image for complete $X$ holds because an isometric image of a complete space is complete.

roles.why: The norm gives the Hahn-Banach functionals and the [dual space](c:dual-space) with its unit ball.
A countable dense set makes the weak-star unit ball a metric space.

steps.slogan: Embed $X$ isometrically in the continuous functions on the dual unit ball.
steps.detail: Let $K$ be the closed unit ball of the [dual space](c:dual-space) $X^*$ with the [weak-star topology](c:weak-star-topology). For each $x$ the Hahn-Banach theorem gives $\varphi \in K$ with $\varphi(x) = \|x\|$. So $\hat{x}(\varphi) = \varphi(x)$ defines a linear map $x \mapsto \hat{x}$ into $C(K)$ with $\sup_K |\hat{x}| = \|x\|$.

steps.slogan: Show that the weak-star unit ball $K$ is a compact metric space.
steps.detail: By the Banach-Alaoglu theorem $K$ is weak-star compact. Let $(x_n)$ be dense in the unit ball of $X$. The metric $d(\varphi, \psi) = \sum_n 2^{-n} |\varphi(x_n) - \psi(x_n)|$ induces the weak-star topology on $K$. So $K$ is a [compact metric space](c:compact-metric-space).

steps.slogan: Pull the functions back along a continuous surjection from the Cantor set.
steps.detail: Every nonempty compact metric space is a continuous image of the [Cantor space](c:cantor-space), so there is a continuous surjection $\pi\colon \Delta \to K$ from the Cantor set $\Delta \subset [0,1]$. The map $g \mapsto g \circ \pi$ from $C(K)$ to $C(\Delta)$ is linear and keeps the supremum norm, because $\pi$ is onto.

steps.slogan: Extend each function on the Cantor set linearly across the gaps.
steps.detail: The set $\Delta$ contains $0$ and $1$, and $[0,1] \setminus \Delta$ is a union of open gaps $(a,b)$ with $a, b \in \Delta$. For $h \in C(\Delta)$ let $Eh = h$ on $\Delta$ and affine from $h(a)$ to $h(b)$ on each gap. Then $Eh$ is continuous, $E$ is linear, and $\sup |Eh| = \sup |h|$.

steps.slogan: Compose the three maps and check that the image is closed.
steps.detail: Put $T x = E(\hat{x} \circ \pi)$. Each factor is linear and keeps the norm, so $\|Tx\|_\infty = \|x\|$. If $X$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space), then $T(X)$ is complete as an isometric copy of $X$, so it is closed in $C[0,1]$.

concepts.c:normed-space: The embedding starts from a norm and its dual space.
concepts.c:c-0-1: The target of the isometry is the space of continuous functions.
concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness of $X$ makes the isometric image closed.
concepts.c:dual-space: The dual space supplies norming functionals and the dual ball.
concepts.c:weak-star-topology: The weak-star topology makes the dual ball compact and metrizable.
concepts.c:compact-metric-space: A compact metric space is a continuous image of the Cantor set.
concepts.c:cantor-space: The Cantor set maps onto the dual ball and sits inside $[0,1]$.

source.note: The Cantor-set proof of the Banach-Mazur theorem (Banach, Theorie des operations lineaires, 1932), as in Albiac and Kalton, Topics in Banach Space Theory.

statement: Let $f\colon X \to S$ be a quasi-compact [separated](c:is-separated) morphism of [schemes](c:scheme), $g\colon S' \to S$ a [flat morphism](c:flat-morphism), $X' = X \times_S S'$ with projections $f', g'$, and $\mathcal{F}$ a [quasi-coherent sheaf](c:is-quasicoherent) on $X$. Then the base change map $g^* R^r f_* \mathcal{F} \to R^r f'_* g'^* \mathcal{F}$ is an isomorphism for every $r \ge 0$.

hypotheses.text: The square with $X' = X \times_S S'$ is a [pullback](c:pullback) of schemes.
The morphism $f$ is quasi-compact and [separated](c:is-separated).
The morphism $g$ is [flat](c:flat-morphism).
The sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$ is [quasi-coherent](c:is-quasicoherent).

conclusion: The base change map from $g^* R^r f_* \mathcal{F}$ to $R^r f'_* g'^* \mathcal{F}$ is an isomorphism of sheaves on $S'$ for all $r \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Cech complex and flatness
proofs.slogan: Compute both sides with one finite affine Cech complex and use that tensoring with a flat module commutes with cohomology.
proofs.scope: Flat base change, one member of the family of base change theorems, for $f$ quasi-compact and separated. Proper base change for torsion sheaves is a separate record.

roles.why: The pullback square gives the affine cover $U_i' = U_i \times_S S'$ of $X'$.
Quasi-compactness gives a finite affine cover, and separatedness makes all intersections affine.
A flat module $B$ keeps the Cech complex exact when tensored.
Quasi-coherence makes sections on affine opens modules that commute with base change.

steps.slogan: Reduce to affine $S = \operatorname{Spec} A$ and affine $S' = \operatorname{Spec} B$.
steps.detail: Both sides are sheaves on $S'$, so it suffices to check on affine opens $\operatorname{Spec} B \subseteq g^{-1}(\operatorname{Spec} A)$ with $\operatorname{Spec} A \subseteq S$ affine. The square restricts to such opens, and $B$ is flat over $A$. For quasi-coherent $\mathcal{F}$, $R^r f_* \mathcal{F}$ is the quasi-coherent sheaf of the $A$-module $H^r(X, \mathcal{F})$.

steps.slogan: Compute the cohomology of $\mathcal{F}$ by a finite affine Cech complex.
steps.detail: Cover $X$ by finitely many affine opens $U_i$, which is possible as $X$ is quasi-compact over affine $S$. Because $f$ is separated, every finite intersection is affine. The [Cech complex](c:cech-cohomology) $C^\bullet$ of $\mathcal{F}$ for this cover is a complex of $A$-modules with $H^r(C^\bullet) = H^r(X, \mathcal{F})$.

steps.slogan: Pull the Cech complex back to the affine cover of $X'$.
steps.detail: The opens $U_i' = U_i \times_S S'$ are affine and cover $X'$, and their finite intersections are affine. On each, $\mathcal{O}$ and $g'^* \mathcal{F}$ have sections $\mathcal{O}(U_{i_0 \cdots i_p}) \otimes_A B$ and $\mathcal{F}(U_{i_0 \cdots i_p}) \otimes_A B$. So the Cech complex of $g'^* \mathcal{F}$ on $X'$ equals $C^\bullet \otimes_A B$.

steps.slogan: Use flatness of $B$ to move the tensor product through cohomology.
steps.detail: Since $B$ is [flat](c:flat-module) over $A$, the functor $- \otimes_A B$ is exact. It therefore commutes with taking cohomology of complexes: $H^r(C^\bullet \otimes_A B) = H^r(C^\bullet) \otimes_A B$.

steps.slogan: Identify the base change map with this isomorphism.
steps.detail: The left side $g^* R^r f_* \mathcal{F}$ is the sheaf of $H^r(X, \mathcal{F}) \otimes_A B$. The right side is the sheaf of $H^r(X', g'^* \mathcal{F}) = H^r(C^\bullet \otimes_A B)$, by step 2 applied to $X'$, which is again quasi-compact and separated over $S'$. The base change map is the natural map between them, which step 4 shows to be bijective.

concepts.c:pullback: The fibre product gives the cover of $X'$ that matches the cover of $X$.
concepts.c:is-separated: Separatedness makes all finite intersections of affine opens affine.
concepts.c:scheme: The statement and the Cech computation live on schemes.
concepts.c:flat-morphism: Flatness of $g$ is the property that keeps cohomology exact under base change.
concepts.c:is-quasicoherent: A quasi-coherent sheaf is determined by modules on affine opens.
concepts.c:cech-cohomology: The Cech complex of a finite affine cover computes the cohomology.
concepts.c:flat-module: Flatness of $B$ over $A$ makes tensoring with $B$ exact.

source.note: The Cech proof of flat base change, as in Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, III, Proposition 9.3; the general quasi-compact quasi-separated case follows from this by Mayer-Vietoris induction.

statement: Let $f\colon [0,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous at $0$, infinitely differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ and completely [monotone](c:monotone-function), that is $(-1)^n f^{(n)} \ge 0$ on $(0,\infty)$ for every $n \ge 0$. Then $f$ is the [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform) of a finite positive [Borel measure](c:borel-measure) $\mu$ on $[0,\infty)$: $f(x) = \int e^{-xs}\, d\mu(s)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is continuous at $0$ and infinitely differentiable on $(0,\infty)$.
The function $f$ is completely [monotone](c:monotone-function): $(-1)^n f^{(n)}(x) \ge 0$ for all $x > 0$ and $n \ge 0$.

conclusion: A finite positive [Borel measure](c:borel-measure) $\mu$ on $[0,\infty)$ has $f(x) = \int_{[0,\infty)} e^{-xs}\, d\mu(s)$ for all $x \ge 0$, and $\mu$ has mass $f(0)$.

proofs.name: Hausdorff moments and Helly selection
proofs.slogan: Sample $f$ on dyadic grids, write each sample sequence as moments of a measure, and take a weak limit of these measures.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Continuity of $f$ at $0$ is used only in the last step, to show that no mass escapes to infinity.

roles.why: Differentiability turns finite differences into integrals of derivatives; continuity at $0$ keeps all mass finite.
The sign of every derivative makes every sampled sequence completely monotone.

steps.slogan: Sample $f$ on the grid $2^{-m}\mathbb{N}$ to get completely monotone sequences.
steps.detail: Fix $m$, let $c = 2^{-m}$ and $a_j = f(jc)$. For $j \ge 1$, the $k$-th difference satisfies $(-1)^k \Delta^k a_j = \int_{[0,c]^k} (-1)^k f^{(k)}(jc + t_1 + \dots + t_k)\, dt \ge 0$. For $j = 0$ let the base point tend to $0$ and use continuity of $f$.

steps.slogan: Write each sample sequence as the moments of a positive measure.
steps.detail: Hausdorff's moment theorem gives a positive Borel measure $\nu_m$ on $[0,1]$ with $a_j = \int u^j\, d\nu_m(u)$ and mass $f(0)$. Put $u = e^{-cs}$, with $u = 0$ for $s = \infty$. This gives a measure $\mu_m$ on $[0,\infty]$ of mass $f(0)$ with $f(j 2^{-m}) = \int e^{-j 2^{-m} s}\, d\mu_m(s)$ for $j \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Select a subsequence of the measures that converges weakly on $[0,\infty]$.
steps.detail: The distribution functions of the $\mu_m$ are monotone and bounded by $f(0)$. Helly's selection theorem gives a subsequence $\mu_{m_k}$ whose distribution functions converge. By the Helly-Bray theorem, $\int h\, d\mu_{m_k} \to \int h\, d\mu$ for every continuous $h$ on the compact space $[0,\infty]$, where $\mu$ has mass $f(0)$.

steps.slogan: Identify $f(x)$ with $\int e^{-xs}\, d\mu$ first for dyadic $x$, then for all $x > 0$.
steps.detail: Let $x = j 2^{-m'}$ with $j \ge 1$. For $m_k \ge m'$ the number $x$ is a positive integer multiple of $2^{-m_k}$, so $f(x) = \int e^{-xs}\, d\mu_{m_k}$. The function $e^{-xs}$ is continuous on $[0,\infty]$ with value $0$ at $\infty$, so $f(x) = \int_{[0,\infty)} e^{-xs}\, d\mu$. Both sides are continuous in $x > 0$, so equality holds for all $x > 0$.

steps.slogan: Let $x$ decrease to $0$ to remove the mass at infinity.
steps.detail: By continuity, $f(x) \to f(0)$. By monotone convergence, $\int_{[0,\infty)} e^{-xs}\, d\mu \to \mu([0,\infty))$. So $\mu([0,\infty)) = f(0) = \mu([0,\infty])$, which gives $\mu(\{\infty\}) = 0$, and the formula also holds at $x = 0$.

concepts.c:monotone-function: Monotonicity of all derivatives makes the sampled sequences completely monotone.
concepts.c:laplace-transform: The integral $\int e^{-xs}\, d\mu$ is the Laplace transform being constructed.
concepts.c:borel-measure: The representing object is a positive Borel measure on the half-line.

source.note: The classical route through Hausdorff's moment theorem and Helly selection, as in Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications II, chapter XIII, and Widder, The Laplace Transform, chapter IV.

statement: Let $M \ne \{0\}$ be a [closed subspace](c:closed-subspace) of the [Hardy space](c:hardy-space) $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ that is invariant under the [shift operator](c:shift-operator) $S f = zf$. Then $M = \theta H^2$ for some [inner function](c:inner-function) $\theta$.

hypotheses.text: The set $M$ is a [closed subspace](c:closed-subspace) of $H^2(\mathbb{D})$.
The subspace $M$ is invariant under the [shift operator](c:shift-operator): $zM \subseteq M$.
The subspace $M$ is not $\{0\}$.

conclusion: There is an [inner function](c:inner-function) $\theta$ with $M = \theta H^2(\mathbb{D})$.

proofs.name: Wandering subspace
proofs.slogan: A unit vector in $M \ominus zM$ is an inner function, and its multiples by $H^2$ fill $M$.
proofs.scope: Beurling's scalar case on the disc. The vector-valued Lax-Halmos form is another member of the family; here $H^2$ is the closed span of $z^n$, $n \ge 0$, in $L^2$ of the circle.

roles.why: A nonzero $M$ is not equal to $zM$, so a wandering vector exists.
Invariance gives $zM \subseteq M$ and puts the multiples $z^n \varphi$ inside $M$.
Closedness makes $zM$ a closed subspace and allows the orthogonal splitting of $M$.

steps.slogan: Find a unit vector $\varphi$ in $M$ orthogonal to $zM$.
steps.detail: Multiplication by $z$ is an isometry of $H^2$, so $zM$ is a closed subspace of $M$. If $zM = M$, then $M = z^n M$ for all $n$, so each $f \in M$ vanishes to order $n$ at $0$ for every $n$ and $f = 0$, against $M \ne \{0\}$. So $M \ominus zM \ne \{0\}$; pick a unit vector $\varphi$ in it.

steps.slogan: Show that $|\varphi| = 1$ almost everywhere on the circle.
steps.detail: For $n \ge 1$ we have $z^n \varphi \in zM$, so $0 = \langle z^n \varphi, \varphi \rangle = \int |\varphi|^2 z^n\, dm$; conjugating treats $n \le -1$. So all nonzero [Fourier coefficients](c:fourier-coefficients) of $|\varphi|^2$ vanish and $|\varphi|^2 = \|\varphi\|^2 = 1$ almost everywhere. Hence $\varphi$ is bounded and [inner](c:inner-function).

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi H^2$ is a closed subspace of $M$.
steps.detail: Because $|\varphi| = 1$, multiplication by $\varphi$ is an isometry of $H^2$, so $\varphi H^2$ is closed. Invariance gives $p \varphi \in M$ for every polynomial $p$. Polynomials are dense in $H^2$, so $\varphi H^2$ is the closure of $\{p\varphi\}$ and lies in $M$.

steps.slogan: Show that no nonzero $g \in M$ is orthogonal to $\varphi H^2$.
steps.detail: Let $g \in M$ with $g \perp z^n \varphi$ for all $n \ge 0$. For $n \ge 1$, $\langle g, z^{-n} \varphi \rangle = \langle z^n g, \varphi \rangle = 0$, as $z^n g \in zM \perp \varphi$. So all Fourier coefficients of $g \bar{\varphi}$ vanish, $g \bar{\varphi} = 0$ almost everywhere, and $|\varphi| = 1$ gives $g = 0$.

steps.slogan: Split $M$ along the closed subspace $\varphi H^2$ to get $M = \varphi H^2$.
steps.detail: Since $\varphi H^2$ is closed in $M$, we have $M = \varphi H^2 \oplus (M \ominus \varphi H^2)$. The second summand is $\{0\}$ by step 4. So $M = \theta H^2$ with $\theta = \varphi$ inner.

concepts.c:closed-subspace: Closedness of $M$ makes $zM$ closed and allows orthogonal decomposition.
concepts.c:hardy-space: The space $H^2$ is where the isometric multiplication by $z$ acts.
concepts.c:shift-operator: Invariance under the shift is the hypothesis that produces $\varphi$ and its multiples.
concepts.c:inner-function: The wandering vector turns out to be an inner function.
concepts.c:fourier-coefficients: Vanishing Fourier coefficients force $|\varphi|^2$ to be constant.

source.note: Beurling, On two problems concerning linear transformations in Hilbert space, Acta Math. 81 (1949), 239-255, with the wandering-subspace argument of Halmos, Shifts on Hilbert spaces, J. reine angew. Math. 208 (1961).

statement: Let $G$ be a connected [solvable](c:solvable-group) [linear algebraic group](c:linear-algebraic-group) over an [algebraically closed field](c:algebraically-closed-field) acting morphically on a nonempty [complete variety](c:complete-variety) $X$, for example a [projective variety](c:projective-variety). Then $G$ has a fixed point in $X$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a connected [solvable](c:solvable-group) [linear algebraic group](c:linear-algebraic-group) over an algebraically closed field.
The variety $X$ is nonempty and [complete](c:complete-variety).
The action $G \times X \to X$ is a morphism of varieties.

conclusion: Some point $x \in X$ satisfies $g x = x$ for all $g \in G$.

proofs.name: Induction on dimension with a closed orbit
proofs.slogan: Reduce to a closed orbit, show that the derived group acts trivially on it, and conclude that the orbit is a complete affine variety, hence a point.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by induction on $\dim G$ with the closed orbit lemma; the case $\dim G = 0$ is trivial. In positive characteristic the identification of an orbit with $G/H$ is the standard one of the cited texts.

roles.why: Solvability makes the derived group a proper connected closed normal subgroup of smaller dimension.
Completeness passes to the closed orbit and rules out a positive-dimensional affine orbit.
A morphic action makes orbits locally closed and stabilizers closed subgroups.

steps.slogan: Induct on $\dim G$ and replace $X$ by a closed [orbit](c:orbit).
steps.detail: If $\dim G = 0$ then $G$ is trivial, since it is connected, and every point is fixed. Let $\dim G > 0$. The boundary of an orbit is a union of orbits of smaller dimension, so an orbit $Y = G \cdot y$ of minimal dimension is closed in $X$, hence complete. It is enough to find a fixed point in $Y$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the derived group, a connected closed normal subgroup of smaller dimension.
steps.detail: The [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup) $G' = [G,G]$ is closed, connected and normal in $G$. It is a proper subgroup, since a solvable $G \ne 1$ has a strictly decreasing derived series. A proper closed subgroup of the irreducible $G$ has smaller dimension, so $\dim G' < \dim G$.

steps.slogan: Apply induction to $G'$ on $Y$ and show that $G'$ acts trivially.
steps.detail: By induction the fixed set $Y^{G'}$ is nonempty. If $y \in Y^{G'}$ and $g \in G$, then $gy$ is fixed by $g G' g^{-1} = G'$. So $Y^{G'}$ is a nonempty $G$-stable subset of the single orbit $Y$, hence $Y^{G'} = Y$.

steps.slogan: Show that all points of $Y$ have the same stabilizer $H$, normal in $G$.
steps.detail: Every stabilizer $G_y$ contains $G'$, and $G_{gy} = g G_y g^{-1}$. Since $G/G'$ is abelian, $g G_y g^{-1} = G_y$. So all stabilizers equal one closed normal subgroup $H$, and $Y$ is the [homogeneous space](c:homogeneous-space) $G/H$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $Y$ is complete, connected and affine, hence a point.
steps.detail: The quotient of a linear algebraic group by a closed normal subgroup is an affine variety, so $Y = G/H$ is affine. It is complete by step 1 and connected as the image of $G$. A complete connected affine variety is a point, and this point is fixed by $G$.

concepts.c:solvable-group: Solvability makes the derived group proper and the induction work.
concepts.c:linear-algebraic-group: The group is an algebraic group whose quotients are affine.
concepts.c:algebraically-closed-field: Algebraic closure is the setting for orbit closure arguments.
concepts.c:complete-variety: Completeness passes to closed orbits and forces a point.
concepts.c:projective-variety: A projective variety is the standard example of a complete variety.
concepts.c:orbit: A closed orbit of minimal dimension is the object to which induction applies.
concepts.c:commutator-subgroup: The derived group is the smaller group that acts trivially on the orbit.
concepts.c:homogeneous-space: The orbit is a quotient $G/H$ with a transitive action.

source.note: Borel, Groupes lineaires algebriques, Annals of Mathematics 64 (1956), 20-82; the induction is the proof in Humphreys, Linear Algebraic Groups, section 21.2.

statement: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) with entries in $\{0,1\}$ and row sums $r_1, \dots, r_n$. Then the [permanent](c:permanent) satisfies $\operatorname{per}(A) \le \prod_{i=1}^n (r_i!)^{1/r_i}$.

hypotheses.text: The [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ is square of size $n$ with every entry equal to $0$ or $1$.
The numbers $r_1, \dots, r_n$ are the row sums of $A$.

proofs.name: Entropy of a random permutation
proofs.slogan: Pick a uniform random permutation counted by the permanent and bound its entropy row by row, in a random order of the rows.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $\operatorname{per}(A) = 0$ there is nothing to prove, so assume $\operatorname{per}(A) \ge 1$; then every $r_i \ge 1$.

roles.why: A $0$-$1$ matrix makes the permanent the number of permutations $\sigma$ with $A_{i\sigma(i)} = 1$ for all $i$.
The row sum $r_i$ is the number of allowed columns of row $i$, which bounds the choices.

steps.slogan: Choose a uniformly random permutation $\sigma$ among those counted by the permanent.
steps.detail: Let $P$ be the set of permutations $\sigma$ with $A_{i\sigma(i)} = 1$ for all $i$. Then $|P| = \operatorname{per}(A)$. For $\sigma$ uniform on $P$, the [entropy](c:entropy) is $H(\sigma) = \log \operatorname{per}(A)$.

steps.slogan: Split the entropy by revealing the rows one at a time in a random order.
steps.detail: For every ordering $\tau$ of the rows, the chain rule gives $H(\sigma) = \sum_i H(\sigma(i) \mid \sigma(j) : \tau(j) < \tau(i))$. Take $\tau$ uniform and independent of $\sigma$; the identity still holds after averaging over $\tau$.

steps.slogan: Bound each term by the logarithm of the number of free columns.
steps.detail: Given the values of $\sigma$ on earlier rows, $\sigma(i)$ lies among the columns of row $i$ that are not yet used; call their number $N_i$. A variable with at most $N$ values has entropy at most $\log N$, by Gibbs' inequality. So each term is at most $E \log N_i$.

steps.slogan: Show that $N_i$ is uniform on $\{1, \dots, r_i\}$ for a fixed $\sigma$.
steps.detail: Row $i$ has $r_i$ columns with entry $1$, and each column is used by exactly one row of $\sigma$. So exactly $r_i$ rows, row $i$ among them, have their column in this set. In a uniform order the number of these rows before row $i$ is uniform on $\{0, \dots, r_i - 1\}$, so $N_i$ is uniform on $\{1, \dots, r_i\}$ and $E \log N_i = \frac{1}{r_i} \log r_i!$.

steps.slogan: Add the bounds over all rows and exponentiate.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 give $\log \operatorname{per}(A) = H(\sigma) \le \sum_i \frac{1}{r_i} \log r_i!$. Exponentiating gives $\operatorname{per}(A) \le \prod_i (r_i!)^{1/r_i}$.

concepts.c:matrix: The permanent and the row sums are defined for the $0$-$1$ matrix.
concepts.c:permanent: The permanent counts the permutations that the random choice ranges over.
concepts.c:entropy: Entropy turns the count of permutations into a sum of row-wise terms.

source.note: Radhakrishnan, An entropy proof of Bregman's theorem, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 77 (1997), 161-164.

statement: Let $p\colon E \to B$ be a [bifibration](c:bifibration) with the [Beck-Chevalley condition](c:beck-chevalley-condition), and $f\colon a \to b$ a morphism with kernel pair and triple fibre product in $B$. For the [monad](c:monad) $T = f^* f_!$ of the [adjunction](c:adjoint-functor) $f_! \dashv f^*$ on $E_a$, the category of $T$-algebras is isomorphic over $E_a$ to the category of [descent data](c:category-of-descent-data) along $f$.

hypotheses.text: The functor $p\colon E \to B$ is a [bifibration](c:bifibration): both a fibration and an opfibration.
The [Beck-Chevalley condition](c:beck-chevalley-condition) holds for the pullback squares of the kernel pair of $f$ and of its triple product.
The kernel pair $a \times_b a$ and the triple fibre product $a \times_b a \times_b a$ exist in $B$.

conclusion: The category of algebras of $T = f^* f_!$ is isomorphic to the category of descent data along $f$, compatibly with the forgetful functors to $E_a$.

proofs.name: Transposing descent data
proofs.slogan: Transpose a descent datum along an adjunction and use Beck-Chevalley to turn it into an algebra structure for the monad.
proofs.scope: The theorem for the kernel pair of $f$. Combined with Beck's monadicity theorem it says that $f$ is of effective descent if and only if $f^*$ is monadic.

roles.why: The bifibration supplies the reindexing functors $f^*$, $p_i^*$ and their left adjoints $f_!$, $p_{2!}$.
Beck-Chevalley identifies $p_{2!} p_1^*$ with $T$ and the triple product with $T^2$.
The kernel pair and triple product are where descent data and their cocycle condition live.

steps.slogan: Define descent data on the kernel pair and the monad of $f_! \dashv f^*$.
steps.detail: Let $c = a \times_b a$ with projections $p_1, p_2$ and diagonal $\Delta$. A descent datum is $(x, \xi)$ with $x \in E_a$, $\xi\colon p_1^* x \to p_2^* x$, $\Delta^* \xi = 1_x$ and the cocycle condition on the triple product. The [monad](c:monad) $T = f^* f_!$ has unit $\eta$ and multiplication $\mu = f^* \varepsilon f_!$.

steps.slogan: Transpose each $\xi$ along the adjunction $p_{2!} \dashv p_2^*$.
steps.detail: Maps $\xi\colon p_1^* x \to p_2^* x$ in $E_c$ correspond bijectively, and naturally in $x$, to maps $\tilde{\xi}\colon p_{2!} p_1^* x \to x$ in $E_a$.

steps.slogan: Replace $p_{2!} p_1^*$ by $T$ using the Beck-Chevalley isomorphism.
steps.detail: The Beck-Chevalley condition for the square $(p_1, p_2, f, f)$ says that the canonical map $p_{2!} p_1^* \to f^* f_!$ is invertible. Composing with it turns $\tilde{\xi}$ into a map $\alpha\colon T x \to x$. This is a bijection between candidate structure maps, natural in $x$.

steps.slogan: Match the unit and cocycle conditions with the algebra axioms.
steps.detail: Under the Beck-Chevalley isomorphisms, the diagonal $\Delta$ turns $\Delta^* \xi = 1_x$ into $\alpha \eta_x = 1_x$. The squares of the triple product identify $T^2$ with the matching composite of reindexings, and the cocycle condition becomes $\alpha \circ T\alpha = \alpha \circ \mu_x$.

steps.slogan: Compare morphisms and read off the isomorphism of categories.
steps.detail: A map $u\colon x \to y$ satisfies $\zeta \, p_1^* u = p_2^* u \, \xi$ if and only if $u \alpha = \beta \, T u$, by naturality of the transposes. So the bijection of objects extends to an isomorphism of categories over $E_a$.

concepts.c:bifibration: A bifibration has reindexing functors with left adjoints.
concepts.c:beck-chevalley-condition: The condition identifies the transposed descent data with monad algebras.
concepts.c:monad: Algebras of the monad $T$ are the objects being compared with descent data.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The adjunction $f_! \dashv f^*$ defines the monad and the transposition.
concepts.c:category-of-descent-data: The descent category is the second side of the isomorphism.
concepts.c:pullback: Kernel pairs and triple products give the base for descent data.

source.note: The theorem is due to Benabou and Roubaud, Monades et descente, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Ser. A-B 270 (1970), A96-A98; the transposition argument is written out here.

statement: Let $(X, d)$ be a nonempty [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space), $\varphi\colon X \to [0,\infty)$ a [lower semicontinuous](c:lower-semicontinuous-function) function and $T\colon X \to X$ a map with $d(x, Tx) \le \varphi(x) - \varphi(Tx)$ for all $x$. Then $T$ has a [fixed point](c:fixed-point).

hypotheses.text: The space $(X, d)$ is a nonempty [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space).
The function $\varphi\colon X \to [0,\infty)$ is [lower semicontinuous](c:lower-semicontinuous-function).
The map $T$ satisfies $d(x, Tx) \le \varphi(x) - \varphi(Tx)$ for every $x \in X$.

conclusion: There is a point $x^* \in X$ with $T x^* = x^*$.

proofs.name: Brondsted order and a minimal point
proofs.slogan: Build a decreasing chain of closed sets with nearly minimal values of $\varphi$, find their limit point, and show that its set is a single point fixed by $T$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, where $T$ need not be continuous; the argument uses the closed sets $S(x) = \{y : d(x,y) \le \varphi(x) - \varphi(y)\}$.

roles.why: Nonemptiness gives a starting point and completeness gives the limit of the Cauchy sequence.
Lower semicontinuity makes the sets $S(x)$ closed and bounds $\varphi$ at the limit.
The inequality says that $Tx^*$ lies in $S(x^*)$.

steps.slogan: Define the sets $S(x)$ and check that they are closed and nested.
steps.detail: Let $S(x) = \{y : d(x,y) + \varphi(y) \le \varphi(x)\}$. It contains $x$, and it is closed because $y \mapsto d(x,y) + \varphi(y)$ is lower semicontinuous. If $y \in S(x)$ and $z \in S(y)$, the triangle inequality gives $d(x,z) \le \varphi(x) - \varphi(z)$, so $S(y) \subseteq S(x)$.

steps.slogan: Choose points $x_{n+1} \in S(x_n)$ with almost minimal value of $\varphi$.
steps.detail: Start at any $x_0 \in X$. Given $x_n$, pick $x_{n+1} \in S(x_n)$ with $\varphi(x_{n+1}) \le \inf_{S(x_n)} \varphi + 2^{-n}$. Then $S(x_{n+1}) \subseteq S(x_n)$ and $\varphi(x_n)$ decreases, so it converges as $\varphi \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $(x_n)$ is a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) with a limit $x^*$.
steps.detail: For $m > n$ we have $x_m \in S(x_n)$, so $d(x_n, x_m) \le \varphi(x_n) - \varphi(x_m)$. This tends to $0$ because $\varphi(x_n)$ converges. By completeness $x_n \to x^*$.

steps.slogan: Show that $S(x^*)$ contains only $x^*$.
steps.detail: The closed set $S(x_n)$ holds all $x_m$ with $m \ge n$, so $x^* \in S(x_n)$ and $S(x^*) \subseteq S(x_n)$. Let $y \in S(x^*)$. Then $\varphi(y) \ge \varphi(x_{n+1}) - 2^{-n}$, and lower semicontinuity gives $\varphi(x^*) \le \varphi(x_{n+1})$. So $d(x^*, y) \le \varphi(x^*) - \varphi(y) \le 2^{-n}$ for all $n$, and $y = x^*$.

steps.slogan: Show that $T x^*$ lies in $S(x^*)$ and conclude that $T x^* = x^*$.
steps.detail: The hypothesis gives $d(x^*, Tx^*) \le \varphi(x^*) - \varphi(Tx^*)$, which says $Tx^* \in S(x^*)$. By step 4, $S(x^*) = \{x^*\}$, so $T x^* = x^*$.

concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness gives the limit of the Cauchy sequence.
concepts.c:lower-semicontinuous-function: Semicontinuity makes the sets $S(x)$ closed and controls the limit value.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The point $x^*$ is the fixed point being found.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: The sequence is Cauchy because the values of $\varphi$ converge.

source.note: Caristi, Fixed point theorems for mappings satisfying inwardness conditions, Transactions of the AMS 215 (1976), 241-251; the nested-set argument follows Ekeland's variational principle.

statement: Let $f$ be an [entire function](c:entire-function) of [exponential type](c:function-of-exponential-type), $|f(z)| \le C e^{\tau |z|}$, with $|f(iy)| \le C e^{c|y|}$ for real $y$, where $c < \pi$. If $f(n) = 0$ for $n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, then $f \equiv 0$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is an [entire function](c:entire-function) with $|f(z)| \le C e^{\tau |z|}$ for all $z$.
On the imaginary axis $|f(iy)| \le C e^{c|y|}$ for all real $y$, with $c < \pi$.
The function vanishes at every integer $n \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Carleman's formula
proofs.slogan: Compare the logarithmic density of the zeros at the integers with Carleman's formula for the half-plane, which allows only $(c/\pi) \log R$ when $c < \pi$.
proofs.scope: The entire case; the half-plane version, with $f$ analytic for $\operatorname{Re} z > 0$ and continuous up to the axis, has the same proof. Zeros of $f$ on the imaginary axis add nothing to the formula.

roles.why: The growth bound controls $\log |f|$ on large half-circles.
The axis bound controls the boundary integral, and $c < \pi$ gives the contradiction.
The zeros at the integers give a left side of size $\log R$.

steps.slogan: Write Carleman's formula for $f \not\equiv 0$ on a half annulus.
steps.detail: Suppose $f \not\equiv 0$ and $C \ge 1$. Fix $\rho \in (1, 3/2)$ and $R > 2$ with no zero of $f$ on $|z| = \rho$ or $|z| = R$. For the zeros $r_k e^{i\theta_k}$ with $\rho < r_k < R$ and $|\theta_k| < \pi/2$, Carleman's formula in the right [half-plane](c:half-plane) states $\sum (r_k^{-1} - r_k R^{-2}) \cos\theta_k = \frac{1}{\pi R} \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \log|f(Re^{i\theta})| \cos\theta\, d\theta + \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_\rho^R (y^{-2} - R^{-2}) \log|f(iy) f(-iy)|\, dy + A(R)$, with $A(R)$ bounded as $R \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: Bound the left side from below by $\log R - K$.
steps.detail: Every term on the left is nonnegative. The zeros $n = 2, \dots, \lfloor R \rfloor$ lie on the positive axis, where $\cos\theta = 1$. They contribute $\sum_n (1/n - n/R^2) \ge \log R - K$ for a constant $K$.

steps.slogan: Bound the arc integral from above by a constant.
steps.detail: Since $\cos\theta \ge 0$ and $\log |f(Re^{i\theta})| \le \log C + \tau R$, the first integral is at most $(\log C + \tau R) \cdot \frac{2}{\pi R}$. This is bounded by a constant $K'$ for $R \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Bound the axis integral from above by $(c/\pi) \log R$ plus a constant.
steps.detail: Here $y^{-2} - R^{-2} \ge 0$ and $\log |f(iy) f(-iy)| \le 2 \log C + 2c y$ for $y > 0$. So the integral is at most $\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_\rho^R y^{-2} (2 \log C + 2cy)\, dy \le \frac{c}{\pi} \log R + K''$.

steps.slogan: Compare the bounds and contradict $c < \pi$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 and the formula give $\log R - K \le \frac{c}{\pi} \log R + K'''$ for all large $R$. So $(1 - c/\pi) \log R$ stays bounded as $R \to \infty$. Since $1 - c/\pi > 0$, this is false, so $f \equiv 0$.

concepts.c:entire-function: Analyticity on the closed half annulus lets Carleman's formula apply.
concepts.c:function-of-exponential-type: The growth bound $e^{\tau|z|}$ makes the arc term bounded.
concepts.c:half-plane: Carleman's formula is the half-plane analogue of Jensen's formula.

source.note: The classical Carleman-formula proof of Carlson's theorem; Carleman's formula and the theorem are treated in Boas, Entire Functions, Academic Press, 1954.

statement: Let $F_k$ be the [Fibonacci numbers](c:fibonacci-numbers) indexed by all integers $k$, with $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and $F_{k+2} = F_{k+1} + F_k$. Then $F_{n+1} F_{n-1} - F_n^2 = (-1)^n$ for every [integer](c:integer) $n$.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $F_k$ satisfy $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$ and $F_{k+2} = F_{k+1} + F_k$ for every integer $k$, which extends them to negative indices.
The index $n$ is an [integer](c:integer), positive, zero or negative.

proofs.name: Induction and reflection
proofs.slogan: Prove the identity for $n \ge 0$ by induction with the recurrence, then reach negative $n$ through the reflection $F_{-k} = (-1)^{k+1} F_k$.
proofs.scope: All integers $n$. The case $n \ge 0$ is an induction, and the case $n < 0$ reduces to it.

roles.why: The recurrence drives the inductive step and gives the reflection formula for negative indices.
The sign of $n$ splits the proof into an induction and a reflection.

steps.slogan: Check the identity at $n = 0$.
steps.detail: The recurrence read backwards gives $F_{-1} = F_1 - F_0 = 1$. So $F_1 F_{-1} - F_0^2 = 1 = (-1)^0$.

steps.slogan: Advance from $n$ to $n + 1$ with the recurrence.
steps.detail: Assume $F_{n+1} F_{n-1} - F_n^2 = (-1)^n$. Using $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$ and $F_{n+1} - F_n = F_{n-1}$ we get $F_{n+2} F_n - F_{n+1}^2 = F_n^2 - F_{n+1}(F_{n+1} - F_n) = F_n^2 - F_{n+1} F_{n-1} = -(-1)^n$. This is $(-1)^{n+1}$, so induction proves all $n \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Prove the reflection formula $F_{-k} = (-1)^{k+1} F_k$.
steps.detail: It holds for $k = 0$ and $k = 1$, because $F_{-1} = 1$. If it holds for $k$ and $k+1$, then $F_{-k-2} = F_{-k} - F_{-k-1} = (-1)^{k+1} F_k - (-1)^{k+2} F_{k+1} = (-1)^{k+3} F_{k+2}$. So induction on $k$ proves the formula.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the case $n = -m < 0$ with the reflection and use the case $m > 0$.
steps.detail: For $m \ge 1$, the reflection gives $F_{1-m} = (-1)^m F_{m-1}$, $F_{-m-1} = (-1)^m F_{m+1}$ and $F_{-m}^2 = F_m^2$. So the expression at $n = -m$ equals $F_{m-1} F_{m+1} - F_m^2 = (-1)^m = (-1)^n$ by the case $m \ge 0$.

concepts.c:fibonacci-numbers: The identity is a statement about consecutive Fibonacci numbers.
concepts.c:integer: The index runs over all integers, which needs the reflection step.

source.note: mathlib proves the case of a natural number by induction with Int.fib_add_two (Int.fib_natCast_succ_mul_fib_natCast_pred_sub_fib_natCast_sq) and reduces negative $n$ to it with Int.fib_neg.

proofs.name: Determinant of the Fibonacci matrix
proofs.slogan: Write $Q^n$ as the matrix of consecutive Fibonacci numbers and take determinants, since $\det Q = -1$.
proofs.scope: All integers $n$, because $Q$ is invertible and the matrix formula holds in both directions of $n$.

roles.why: The recurrence shows that the matrix of Fibonacci numbers is multiplied by $Q$ at each step.
The power $Q^n$ is defined for every integer $n$ because $Q$ is invertible.

steps.slogan: Show that $Q^n$ is the matrix of consecutive Fibonacci numbers.
steps.detail: Let $Q$ be the [matrix](c:matrix) with rows $(1, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$, and $M_n$ the matrix with rows $(F_{n+1}, F_n)$ and $(F_n, F_{n-1})$. Then $M_0 = I$, and $M_n Q = M_{n+1}$ and $Q^{-1} M_n = M_{n-1}$ by the recurrence. So $Q^n = M_n$ for every integer $n$.

steps.slogan: Compute $\det Q^n$ from $\det Q = -1$ by multiplicativity.
steps.detail: The [determinant](c:determinant) of $Q$ is $-1$, so $Q$ is invertible. Since the determinant is multiplicative, $\det Q^n = (\det Q)^n = (-1)^n$ for every integer $n$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\det M_n$ and equate it with $(-1)^n$.
steps.detail: The determinant of $M_n$ is $F_{n+1} F_{n-1} - F_n^2$. Since $M_n = Q^n$, this equals $(-1)^n$.

concepts.c:fibonacci-numbers: The matrix $Q^n$ has consecutive Fibonacci numbers as entries.
concepts.c:integer: The matrix formula is proved for every integer exponent.
concepts.c:matrix: The Fibonacci matrix $Q$ encodes the recurrence.
concepts.c:determinant: The determinant is multiplicative and gives the sign $(-1)^n$.

source.note: The classical matrix proof of Cassini's identity with the Fibonacci Q-matrix.

statement: Let $P$ and $P'$ be [convex polyhedra](c:convex-polyhedron) in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with a combinatorial equivalence under which corresponding faces are congruent. Then $P$ and $P'$ are congruent, by an isometry of space that may reverse orientation.

hypotheses.text: The solids $P$ and $P'$ are [convex polyhedra](c:convex-polyhedron) in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
A bijection of vertices, edges and faces from $P$ to $P'$ preserves incidence.
Corresponding faces are [congruent](c:congruence-in-geometry), with corresponding vertices matched.

conclusion: An isometry of $\mathbb{R}^3$ maps $P$ onto $P'$ and respects the correspondence.

proofs.name: Cauchy's sign-change count
proofs.slogan: Compare dihedral angles edge by edge, count sign changes around vertices and around regions, and show by Euler's formula that all angles agree.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in Cauchy's argument with Steinitz's correction of the sign lemma. Generalizations to non-convex or flexible polyhedra are separate results.

roles.why: Convexity makes each vertex figure a convex spherical polygon, which the sign lemma needs.
The bijection lets us compare the same edge, vertex and face in $P$ and $P'$.
Congruent faces give equal edge lengths and equal face angles.

steps.slogan: Label each edge by comparing its [dihedral angle](c:dihedral-angle) in $P$ and $P'$.
steps.detail: Congruent faces give equal edge lengths and equal face angles. Label an edge $+$ if its dihedral angle in $P'$ is larger than in $P$, $-$ if smaller and $0$ if equal. Steps 2 to 4 show that no edge carries $+$ or $-$.

steps.slogan: Show that a vertex with a nonzero edge has at least four sign changes.
steps.detail: A small sphere around a vertex cuts $P$ and $P'$ in convex spherical polygons with equal sides (the face angles) and the dihedral angles as vertex angles. If the polygons differ, Cauchy's arm lemma shows that the cyclic signs of the angle differences, zeros removed, change at least four times. Fewer changes would split the polygon into two arms with opposite strict distance inequalities.

steps.slogan: Bound the sign changes around each region of the graph of nonzero edges.
steps.detail: Let $H$ be the graph of edges labeled $+$ or $-$, drawn on the sphere. By step 2 every vertex of $H$ has degree at least $4$, so every region has $d \ge 3$ corners. Going around a region the number of sign changes is even and at most $d$, so at most $d - 1$ when $d$ is odd.

steps.slogan: Count the sign changes two ways and use Euler's formula to get a contradiction.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be the total number of sign changes at corners, with $V$, $E$ and $F$ the numbers of vertices, edges and regions of $H$ and $f_{\mathrm{odd}}$ the regions of odd degree. Step 2 gives $S \ge 4V$ and step 3 gives $S \le 2E - f_{\mathrm{odd}}$. Euler's formula $V - E + F \ge 2$ for the planar graph $H$ then gives $8 + \sum_f (d_f - 4) + f_{\mathrm{odd}} \le 0$. But $d_f - 4 < 0$ only for triangles, which are odd, so the left side is at least $8$.

steps.slogan: Glue the congruent faces along equal dihedral angles to get the isometry.
steps.detail: By step 4 every edge has label $0$, so corresponding faces meet at equal dihedral angles. Map one face of $P$ onto its partner by an isometry. An adjacent face is congruent to its partner and meets at the same angle, so it maps onto its partner too. The face graph is connected, so one isometry maps $P$ onto $P'$.

concepts.c:convex-polyhedron: Convexity makes the vertex figures convex spherical polygons.
concepts.c:congruence-in-geometry: Congruent faces give equal side lengths and face angles at each vertex.
concepts.c:dihedral-angle: The dihedral angles are the quantities that the sign labels compare.

source.note: Cauchy (1813) with Steinitz's repair of the sign lemma, as in Aigner and Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK, chapter on Cauchy's rigidity theorem.

statement: Let $C_1, C_2$ be [cubic curves](c:cubic-curve) in the complex projective plane that meet in nine distinct points $p_1, \dots, p_9$. If a cubic curve passes through $p_1, \dots, p_8$, then it passes through $p_9$.

hypotheses.text: The curves $C_1 = V(F_1)$ and $C_2 = V(F_2)$ are [cubic curves](c:cubic-curve) in $\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C})$.
The intersection $C_1 \cap C_2$ consists of nine distinct points $p_1, \dots, p_9$.
A cubic curve $V(G)$ contains $p_1, \dots, p_8$.

proofs.name: Global residue theorem
proofs.slogan: Move to affine coordinates, show that the nine points are simple, and use the vanishing of the sum of residues of a cubic over the two cubics.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem over $\mathbb{C}$. Cayley-Bacharach is a family: this is the plane cubic case, and the general case for curves of degrees $d$ and $e$ and curves of degree $d + e - 3$ has the same proof.

roles.why: Degree $3$ for both curves gives the degree bound $3 + 3 - 3 = 3$ for the Euler-Jacobi formula.
Nine distinct points and Bezout make every intersection simple, so the Jacobian does not vanish.
Vanishing at eight points leaves one term in the residue sum.

steps.slogan: Choose affine coordinates in which all nine points are finite and the curves meet only there.
steps.detail: Pick a line missing all $p_i$, which exists over an infinite field, and take it as the line at infinity. Let $f_1, f_2, g$ be the dehomogenized polynomials of $F_1, F_2, G$, of degree at most $3$. The curves have no common point at infinity, because $C_1 \cap C_2 = \{p_1, \dots, p_9\}$.

steps.slogan: Show that every $p_i$ is a simple intersection point, so the Jacobian is nonzero there.
steps.detail: The curves have no common component, since they meet in finitely many points. By Bezout's theorem the intersection numbers add up to $9$. There are nine points, so each has multiplicity $1$. Hence the curves are smooth at $p_i$ with distinct tangents, and $J = \det \partial(f_1, f_2)/\partial(x, y)$ is nonzero at $p_i$.

steps.slogan: Apply the Euler-Jacobi formula, the global [residue](c:residue) theorem for two cubics.
steps.detail: Let $f_1, f_2$ have only simple common zeros $p_i$, none at infinity. For every polynomial $h$ of degree at most $3 + 3 - 3 = 3$, $\sum_{i=1}^9 h(p_i)/J(p_i) = 0$. This is the vanishing of the sum of the residues of $h\, dx \wedge dy/(f_1 f_2)$, which holds because this form has no residue at infinity in this degree range.

steps.slogan: Insert the given cubic and read off its value at the ninth point.
steps.detail: Take $h = g$. The cubic vanishes at $p_1, \dots, p_8$, so eight terms of the sum are zero. This leaves $g(p_9)/J(p_9) = 0$. Since $J(p_9) \ne 0$, we get $g(p_9) = 0$, so $p_9$ lies on the cubic.

concepts.c:cubic-curve: Both given curves and the test curve are plane cubics.
concepts.c:residue: The vanishing of the residue sum is the engine of the proof.

source.note: The residue proof of Cayley-Bacharach, as in Griffiths and Harris, Principles of Algebraic Geometry (1978), section on residues; Eisenbud, Green and Harris, Cayley-Bacharach theorems and conjectures, Bull. AMS 33 (1996), treat the theorem in depth.

statement: Let $M$ be a complete $n$-dimensional [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) with [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) at least $(n-1)k$, let $p \in M$ and $R > 0$, with $R \le \pi/\sqrt{k}$ if $k > 0$. Then the first [Dirichlet eigenvalue](c:dirichlet-eigenvalue) of the [Laplace-Beltrami operator](c:laplace-beltrami-operator) on the geodesic ball $B(p, R)$ is at most that of a ball of radius $R$ in the space form of curvature $k$.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is a complete [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of dimension $n \ge 2$.
The [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) satisfies $\operatorname{Ric} \ge (n-1)k$ on $M$.
The radius satisfies $R > 0$, and $R \le \pi/\sqrt{k}$ when $k > 0$.

conclusion: The first Dirichlet eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda_1(B(p,R)) \le \lambda_1(B_k(R))$, where $B_k(R)$ is the model ball of radius $R$.

proofs.name: Radial test function and volume comparison
proofs.slogan: Transplant the radial first eigenfunction of the model ball as a test function, and compare the Rayleigh quotients by Bishop's area comparison.
proofs.scope: The Ricci-lower-bound member of the family of Cheng's comparison theorems, with an upper bound on $\lambda_1$. The sectional-curvature upper bound with a lower bound on $\lambda_1$ is a separate member.

roles.why: Completeness makes the exponential map at $p$ defined on all of $B(p, R)$, so polar coordinates cover the ball.
The Ricci bound gives Bishop's comparison of the area functions.
The radius bound makes the model ball a true ball with a radial first eigenfunction.

steps.slogan: Take the radial first eigenfunction $v$ of the model ball.
steps.detail: In the space form of curvature $k$ let $A_k(r)$ be the area of the sphere of radius $r$. The first Dirichlet eigenfunction of the model ball is radial, $v(r)$, with $v > 0$ on $[0, R)$, $v(R) = 0$ and $(A_k v')' = -\lambda_k A_k v$ for $\lambda_k = \lambda_1(B_k(R))$. Because $A_k v' \to 0$ at $0$ and decreases, $v' \le 0$.

steps.slogan: Transplant $v$ to $B(p,R)$ as the test function $\phi = v \circ d_p$.
steps.detail: The function $\phi$ is Lipschitz and vanishes on $\partial B(p,R)$, and $|\nabla d_p| = 1$ almost everywhere. The variational characterization of $\lambda_1$ gives $\lambda_1(B(p,R)) \le \int |\nabla \phi|^2 / \int \phi^2 = \int_0^R v'^2 A\, dr \big/ \int_0^R v^2 A\, dr$. Here $A(r)$ is the area of the part of the sphere of radius $r$ inside the cut locus, in geodesic polar coordinates.

steps.slogan: Compare the area functions by Bishop's volume comparison.
steps.detail: Under $\operatorname{Ric} \ge (n-1)k$, the ratio $h(r) = A(r)/A_k(r)$ is non-increasing on $(0, R)$ with $h(0^+) = 1$. The cut locus only lowers $A$, because the set of directions whose geodesics are still minimizing at radius $r$ shrinks as $r$ grows.

steps.slogan: Show that $W(s) = \int_0^s (v'^2 - \lambda_k v^2) A_k\, dr$ is at most $0$ and vanishes at $R$.
steps.detail: Integrate by parts with $(A_k v')' = -\lambda_k A_k v$: $\int_0^s v'^2 A_k\, dr = v(s) v'(s) A_k(s) + \lambda_k \int_0^s v^2 A_k\, dr$. So $W(s) = v(s) v'(s) A_k(s) \le 0$, since $v \ge 0 \ge v'$, and $W(R) = 0$ because $v(R) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Integrate by parts against the non-increasing ratio $h$ to compare the quotients.
steps.detail: We have $\int_0^R (v'^2 - \lambda_k v^2) A\, dr = \int_0^R h\, dW = -\int_0^R W\, dh \le 0$, because $hW = 0$ at both ends, $W \le 0$ and $h$ is non-increasing. So $\int v'^2 A \le \lambda_k \int v^2 A$, and step 2 gives $\lambda_1(B(p,R)) \le \lambda_k$.

concepts.c:riemannian-manifold: Geodesic polar coordinates and the cut locus live on the manifold.
concepts.c:ricci-curvature: A lower Ricci bound is what Bishop's comparison needs.
concepts.c:dirichlet-eigenvalue: The first Dirichlet eigenvalue is the quantity being compared.
concepts.c:laplace-beltrami-operator: The eigenvalue is that of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on the ball.

source.note: Cheng, Eigenvalue comparison theorems and its geometric applications, Math. Z. 143 (1975), 289-297; see also Chavel, Eigenvalues in Riemannian Geometry, chapter III.

statement: Let $a < b$ and let $\delta\colon [a,b] \to (0,\infty)$ be any function. Then there is a [tagged partition](c:tagged-partition) $a = x_0 < \dots < x_n = b$ with tags $t_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$ and $[x_{i-1}, x_i] \subset (t_i - \delta(t_i), t_i + \delta(t_i))$ for all $i$.

hypotheses.text: The set $[a,b]$ is a closed bounded [interval](c:interval) with $a < b$.
The function $\delta$ is positive at every point; no continuity is assumed.

proofs.name: Bisection
proofs.slogan: Assume that no fine partition exists, halve the interval repeatedly, and use the gauge at the common point to build one.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $a < b$ (for $a = b$ one tagged point suffices). Call a tagged partition $\delta$-fine if each $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$ lies in $(t_i - \delta(t_i), t_i + \delta(t_i))$.

roles.why: A closed bounded interval can be halved into closed intervals that shrink to a point.
Positivity of $\delta$ at $c$ makes small intervals around $c$ fine with the tag $c$.

steps.slogan: Assume that $[a,b]$ has no $\delta$-fine tagged partition.
steps.detail: Suppose, for contradiction, that no [tagged partition](c:tagged-partition) of $[a,b]$ is $\delta$-fine. The same property is then tested on every subinterval that the next steps produce.

steps.slogan: Halve the interval repeatedly, keeping a half with no fine partition.
steps.detail: If both halves of an interval $I$ had $\delta$-fine partitions, their union would be a $\delta$-fine partition of $I$. So one half has none. This gives nested closed intervals $I_n = [a_n, b_n]$ of length $(b - a) 2^{-n}$ with $I_0 = [a,b]$, none having a fine partition.

steps.slogan: Take the common point $c$ of the nested intervals.
steps.detail: The left ends $a_n$ increase and the right ends $b_n$ decrease with $a_n \le b_n$. By the nested intervals lemma, $c = \sup a_n$ lies in every $I_n$.

steps.slogan: Use the gauge at $c$ to build a fine partition of a small $I_n$.
steps.detail: Choose $n$ with $(b - a) 2^{-n} < \delta(c)$. Since $c \in I_n$, we get $I_n \subset (c - \delta(c), c + \delta(c))$. So the one-interval partition of $I_n$ with tag $c$ is $\delta$-fine.

steps.slogan: Compare with the choice of $I_n$ to contradict the assumption.
steps.detail: Step 4 gives a $\delta$-fine partition of $I_n$, against step 2. So the assumption fails, and $[a,b]$ has a $\delta$-fine tagged partition.

concepts.c:tagged-partition: A tagged partition with intervals inside the gauge neighborhoods is the object sought.
concepts.c:interval: The closed interval is the compact set that bisection exhausts.

source.note: Cousin's original bisection argument, as presented in Gordon, The Integrals of Lebesgue, Denjoy, Perron, and Henstock, AMS (1994).

statement: Consider a logic with [modus ponens](c:modus-ponens), conditional proof that may use an assumption twice ([contraction](c:contraction-rule)), and unrestricted [comprehension](c:axiom-of-full-comprehension): each formula $\varphi(x)$ gives a set $\{x : \varphi(x)\}$ with $y \in \{x : \varphi(x)\} \leftrightarrow \varphi(y)$. Then every sentence $A$ is derivable.

hypotheses.text: The logic has [modus ponens](c:modus-ponens): from $B$ and $B \to C$ derive $C$.
The logic has conditional proof: if $C$ follows from an assumption $B$, then $B \to C$ holds. The assumption may be used more than once ([contraction](c:contraction-rule)).

The logic has unrestricted [comprehension](c:axiom-of-full-comprehension): for every formula $\varphi$ there is a set $\{x : \varphi(x)\}$ with $y \in \{x : \varphi(x)\}$ equivalent to $\varphi(y)$ by implications in both directions.

conclusion: Every sentence $A$ has a derivation, so the logic is trivial.

proofs.name: The Curry set
proofs.slogan: Form the set of all $x$ with $x \in x \to A$, and derive $A$ from its membership equivalence using contraction once.
proofs.scope: Any logic with the three rules, such as naive set theory over classical logic. The argument does not apply without contraction or with restricted comprehension.

roles.why: Modus ponens turns the membership implication and the assumption into $A$.
Conditional proof, with the assumption used twice, discharges the assumption.
Comprehension gives the Curry set and its membership equivalence in both directions.

steps.slogan: Form the Curry set $X = \{x : x \in x \to A\}$ for an arbitrary sentence $A$.
steps.detail: Take any sentence $A$. [Comprehension](c:axiom-of-full-comprehension) gives the set $X$ with the equivalence $(*)$: $X \in X \leftrightarrow (X \in X \to A)$.

steps.slogan: Assume $X \in X$ and derive $A$.
steps.detail: From the assumption $X \in X$ and $(*)$ we get $X \in X \to A$. Then [modus ponens](c:modus-ponens) with the assumption $X \in X$ gives $A$. The assumption is used twice.

steps.slogan: Discharge the assumption to prove $X \in X \to A$ outright.
steps.detail: Conditional proof turns the derivation of step 2 into a proof of $X \in X \to A$ from no assumptions. This uses the assumption twice, so it needs [contraction](c:contraction-rule).

steps.slogan: Turn the implication back into the membership $X \in X$.
steps.detail: By $(*)$ in the backward direction, the theorem $X \in X \to A$ of step 3 gives $X \in X$, again from no assumptions.

steps.slogan: Combine the two theorems by modus ponens to derive $A$.
steps.detail: We have $X \in X$ from step 4 and $X \in X \to A$ from step 3. Modus ponens gives $A$ from no assumptions. Since $A$ was arbitrary, every sentence is derivable.

concepts.c:modus-ponens: Modus ponens produces $A$ from the implication and its antecedent.
concepts.c:contraction-rule: Contraction lets the assumption $X \in X$ be used twice in one derivation.
concepts.c:axiom-of-full-comprehension: Unrestricted comprehension creates the self-referential Curry set.

source.note: Curry, The inconsistency of certain formal logics, Journal of Symbolic Logic 7 (1942), 115-117.
